findings.claim: They argued that the family had passed through three historical stages and was now entering a fourth, characterised by the symmetrical family.
findings.truth: Young and Willmott's symmetrical family is Stage 3, the home-centred nuclear family they said had already arrived. Their Stage 4 is the 'managing director' family, which is work-centred, with the wife responsible for home and children. The lesson moves the symmetrical family into Stage 4 and so reverses their model. A student who repeated this would describe Young and Willmott's own stages wrongly.
findings.evidence: spec 7.1 key thinkers, Willmott and Young 1973: 'Young and Wilmott used the term symmetrical family to describe the Stage 3 (home centred) nuclear family... The managing director family (Stage 4) cited in their research was work-centred rather than home-centred'

findings.claim: what Willmott and Young called privatised instrumentalism (repeated in the flashcard answer and the glossary definition, both of which open 'Willmott and Young's term for...')
findings.truth: Privatised instrumentalism comes from the Affluent Worker studies of Goldthorpe, Lockwood, Bechhofer and Platt (1968-69), not from Young and Willmott. The AQA spec lists it as a key term with no author attached, and its own summary of Young and Willmott names only the symmetrical family, stratified diffusion and the managing director family. Attaching the term to a named spec thinker who did not coin it is a false attribution.
findings.evidence: spec 6.1 key terms 'Privatised instrumentalism (social relationships centred on the home)' - unattributed; spec 7.1 Willmott and Young summary does not use the term; Wikipedia, John H. Goldthorpe (Affluent Worker studies with Lockwood, Bechhofer and Platt, 1968-69)

findings.claim: Subsequent legal changes, including the introduction of legal aid for divorce cases, further reduced the practical barriers to obtaining a divorce.
findings.truth: Legal aid for divorce came in under the Legal Aid and Advice Act 1949, well before the Divorce Reform Act 1969, so it is not a 'subsequent' change; and legal aid for most divorce cases in England and Wales was withdrawn in 2013. The genuine later legal change is the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020, in force 6 April 2022, which introduced no-fault divorce. The spec requires 'changes in the law' as a reason for the rise in divorce, and the lesson's legal history stops in 1971.
findings.evidence: spec 3.3.6 'explain reasons for the rise in divorce since 1945 including: changes in the law'; Wikipedia, Divorce in England and Wales: 'No-fault divorce became law on 6 April 2022 under the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020'

findings.claim: Willmott and Young's research for The Symmetrical Family (1973) used large-scale surveys to gather data from hundreds of households
findings.truth: The spec gives the sample: nearly 2,000 people interviewed in Greater London and the surrounding areas. 'Hundreds' understates it by roughly an order of magnitude, and this lesson is about judging method and sample size, so the wrong figure undermines the point it is making.
findings.evidence: spec 7.1 key thinkers: 'based on a large scale social survey (nearly 2,000 people were interviewed in Greater London and surrounding areas)'

findings.claim: Oakley developed the concept of the double shift (repeated in lesson 3 flashcards, a lesson 3 knowledge check and lesson 6 content as 'Oakley's double shift')
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Leave it: the spec lists 'Double shift (women in marriage)' as a families key term with no author, Oakley is the named feminist for this part of the spec, and every mainstream GCSE textbook pairs Oakley with the dual burden or double shift, so a student writing it would not be marked wrong. (b) De-attribute across four places: Oakley's 1974 housework research documents the burden but the phrase is not her coinage (the second-shift formulation is Hochschild, 1989; the triple shift is Duncombe and Marsden, 1995). Recommendation: leave it, and de-attribute only if the fleet adopts a general rule against unsourced concept attributions.
findings.evidence: spec 6.1 key terms 'Double shift (women in marriage)' - unattributed; spec 7.1 Oakley summary (Conventional families, 1982) does not use the phrase
findings.ruling: NOTE: 'double shift' left attributed to Oakley - spec lists the term unattributed, Oakley is its named feminist here; no student would lose a mark.

findings.claim: In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare - around 25,000 divorces per year.
findings.truth: About 25,000 a year is a fair figure for the 1950s, but the decade straight after the war opens with a large post-war spike (1947 is normally given as roughly 60,000 in England and Wales) as wartime marriages were dissolved. 'In the 1950s' would carry the same number safely. Not edited: the ONS bulletins reachable this session carry no pre-1970 series, so the true 1947 value was not sourced.
findings.evidence: ONS Divorces in England and Wales bulletins 2021 and 2022 - no long-run series before 1971; WebSearch budget exhausted

findings.claim: The Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church had traditionally taught that marriage was a lifelong sacrament
findings.truth: True of the Roman Catholic Church. For the Church of England, Article XXV counts matrimony among the five rites 'commonly called Sacraments' that it does not number among the two Sacraments of the Gospel. 'Lifelong' is right for both; 'sacrament' is loose for the Anglican half. The sociological point is unaffected, so no edit.

findings.claim: The Rapoports' research on family diversity involved extensive contact with families over time, using a mixed methods approach combining interviews with observational elements.
findings.truth: The Rapoports did run intensive dual-career family studies, but the piece the spec sets, 'British families in transition' (1982), is a review chapter rather than a fieldwork report, and no source found this session describes an observational component. The claim is plausible but unsourced. Left alone because it is offered as background, not as an examinable fact.
findings.evidence: spec 7.1 Rapoport and Rapoport 1982 entry, which describes the five aspects of diversity and no method

summary: One HIGH error: lesson 4 makes the symmetrical family Young and Willmott's fourth stage when the spec's own key-thinker text puts it at Stage 3 and gives Stage 4 to the work-centred managing director family. Three MEDIUM fixes follow: privatised instrumentalism wrongly attributed to Willmott and Young in three fields of lesson 4, legal aid presented as a post-1969 change in lesson 6 with the 2022 no-fault reform absent, and Young and Willmott's sample shrunk to 'hundreds of households' in lesson 7. Every practice question sits on the 1/2/3/4/12 ladder, no lesson asserts a paper, section, timing or SPaG claim, and all 35 knowledge-check keys recompute correct.
